name: Iceland
summary:
Iceland is a Nordic island nation in the North Atlantic, straddling the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between the Eurasian and North American tectonic plates. With 370,000 people on 103,000 km², Iceland is the world's most sparsely populated country in Europe and one of the most geologically active territories on Earth — shaped by volcanic eruptions, geothermal vents, and glaciers. It ranks among the most developed countries in the world by every human development metric.

Norse settlement of Iceland began c. 874 CE, according to the Landnámabók (Book of Settlements), led by Ingólfr Arnarson. The Althing, established in 930 CE, is the world's oldest parliament still in operation — a democratic assembly of chieftains that governed Iceland for over three centuries. The Icelandic sagas — literary masterworks composed in the 13th–14th centuries — are among the most significant literary productions of medieval Europe, providing unique insights into Viking-age Scandinavia, exploration (including the discovery of North America by Leif Erikson c. 1000 CE), and early medieval society.

Iceland came under Norwegian (1262) and then Danish (1381) sovereignty, becoming independent in 1944 during World War II. Its strategic position led to US basing during the Cold War. Modern Iceland has transformed geothermal energy into near-100% renewable electricity and heating — a model for sustainable energy. The 2008 financial crisis hit Iceland catastrophically (its banks' liabilities were 10× GDP), but the country's decision to let banks fail and prosecute bankers rather than impose austerity resulted in faster recovery than most European peers.

Its longevity and adaptability have made it a model for democratic assemblies worldwide.
